uniequip_003_reed2.desc.text:
"...According to the latest report from the Catastrophe Messengers, the summer flight path of the Nasr Sha has been replanned—
"Ah, right."
The figure buried behind the desk, listening to reports and reviewing applications all the while, finally looked up from the mountain of documents.
"Before moving onto the new route, what should we do about those empty houses on the derelict plate?"

Nemesis walked into the office carrying the day's latest newspapers, which included a trial issue written in Tarann alongside the standard daily papers still printed in Victorian. Normally, they would be neatly arranged on the newspaper rack and replaced every day. This wasn't supposed to be her job, but ever since Loughshinny began submitting anonymous pieces to the press, she had to pay utmost attention to these flimsy sheets of paper.
Today, before reaching the rack, her steps hesitated. "What's that?"
Noticing the secretary's gaze, Loughshinny turned her eyes toward her elbow. An object taking up a full third of the desk sat quietly there.
"Hmm, it's a... 'model house'? At least, that's what the person who delivered it called it." The Draco touched the decorative flowers on the model's base.
"Oh, could it be a design for the reconstruction of the old houses? I thought they were merely talking." Nemesis set the papers down and stepped forward, lightly stroking the model's 'roof,' only to find that even the tiles had been stacked layer by layer. "After all, the priority is repairing those ruined buildings so they are livable again. Aesthetics should be the last thing on the list."
"I understand. But this is probably a kind of... hope? Maybe one day, every Taran will be able to live in a house like this." As if recalling something, a faint smile appeared on Loughshinny's face.
Nemesis smiled as well, then shook her head.
"No, I don't think that's all they meant." With that, she pushed open one of the small windows, reached inside, fumbled around for a moment, and finally pulled her hand back in a clenched fist, as though grasping something.

"...Leaving them empty feels like a waste. Why not turn them into an orphanage? For the orphans who lost their families in the war and have no one to raise them. I can provide the seed money, from my own personal—"
"Your Highness."
"—Yes, and my salary, isn't it all in the public welfare fund? We can just withdraw it—"
"Loughshinny."
The person whose name was called trembled slightly.
"If this is what you wish, we will all stand behind you. For those left behind in the war—be they people or houses—we will find a proper way to settle them.
"You don't always have to bear everything alone."

Nemesis opened her hand, revealing two brass keys and a slip of paper with an address written on it. Her smile carried a touch of nostalgia.
"I used to think that once the war was over, we could naturally return to our normal lives. Moving into a new house with family seemed like a fine place to start."
Loughshinny stood up, wanting to walk over to Nemesis, wanting to say something. But what could she say? About Theo, about Colin, even about her sister... even about Eblana? She realized she didn't know where to begin, so she remained silent.
The red-haired Feline reached out, persistently holding the keys forward.
"It seems those children hold the same blessing for you, Princess Loughshinny. So please, accept it.
"Besides, this address happens to be right next to the newly built orphanage."

uniequip_003_yato2.desc.text:
Deep in the mountains of Higashi, there was once an Oni girl.
The village she came from was renowned for its fierce mercenaries, and her parents were among the very best of them. Thus, the path of her life was decided the moment she was born.
Slash, thrust, parry. Day after day, year after year.
Until the day she packed her bags and left home.
Bad people, cut down. Good people, cut down.
The weak, cut down. The strong, with some effort, cut down all the same.
Aside from the sensation of blade cutting into flesh, she knew nothing of others.
Until she was hired, and stood on the opposing side of a green-haired woman.
...
Amidst the ruins of Kazdel, there was an Oni mercenary.
She was once a captive, but accepted the offer of surrender.
The woman known as the Lord of Fiends praised her martial skill, and asked her not to slaughter every foe, but to hold the ground here. And so, Babel gained a silent gatekeeper.
When blood-soaked Sarkaz scouts rushed back to the gates, she stayed behind to cover their retreat; when the leaders fell silent in late-night meetings, she quietly lit the candles.
She sat on the same chair for hundreds of days and nights, wiping down her blade far more often than she swung it.
Until that day, when she was dispatched to provide cover on the perimeter. By the time she fought her way back through smoke and gunfire, everything was already settled.
Without much sorrow, she simply sheathed her blade out of habit. Since she was still alive, she would find another place to stand guard.
...
Aboard Rhodes Island, there was an Oni operator.
No one knew when she joined Rhodes Island, and no one particularly cared. Her presence on the landship was taken for granted, and everyone assumed she would simply remain here forever.
During Rhodes Island's reconstruction, her daily routine grew exceedingly regular.
Correcting recruits' sword grips; patrolling the bridge, checking every surveillance blind spot; actively participating in field missions, clearing obstacles for Rhodes Island.
Occasionally, she would silently gaze at the barren wasteland outside the ship's windows. She felt nothing in particular, only that the blade seemed lighter.
Until that day, when she was assigned to an investigation mission in Luohua Village.
...
"Instructor, in the end, did hunting teach you the meaning behind swinging your weapon?"
Facing the question from her new students, she couldn't help but sigh.
"Things like that aren't so easy to find, and besides..."
"Besides?"
"The day after I returned from Luohua Village, I intended to put my mask back on, but I found it had broken. The material was unique, and repairs took quite a while."
"And then?"
"And then I had to run around squinting my eyes, with every passerby staring straight at my face. But over those few days, I gradually grew used to it."
"Isn't that great? Everyone feels Instructor Yato is much friendlier now."
Yato thought to herself: whether it was hunting or taking off the mask, neither truly changed who she was. It was just that certain words were no longer so difficult to speak.
With that thought, she walked to the center of the training ground.
"Alright, recruits, class is starting. I am your instructor, Yato. That is my codename, and my name. Starting today, I will teach you the techniques of using dual blades and the long sword."

uniequip_003_blaze2.desc.text:
"'It's fine,' but that doesn't mean nothing happened. Maybe they really don't mind, or maybe they mind terribly, but choose not to say anything. Maybe they stay silent because they're too close to you and don't want to hurt your feelings. Or maybe it's because they barely know you and don't want to waste their breath.
"'Do as you see fit.' Sounds like they're letting you decide, but it could be a sign of trust, or a sign of disdain and brush-off. If it's the former, you ultimately still have to defer to what they want to show your gratitude and respect. If it's the latter, it's even worse—not only can you not act on your own, you also have to figure out how you offended them in the first place—
"This is giving me a headache!
"Compared to these people, even those cave rodents in the desert that only squeak once in their lives seem chatty!"
Blaze snapped the pen in her hand, splattering ink all over herself. Letting out a long sigh, she rummaged around the guest room for ages, only managing to find the Tianshi-style outfit Leizi had prepared for her.
"It's all Lin Qingyan's fault for not warning me beforehand. Not only did I make a fool of myself in the streets, now I even have to write my own cheat sheet for talking to people!" Thinking back to what happened on the streets of Baizao over the past few days, Blaze rubbed her temples in exasperation.
"Next time I see people arguing and shoving in front of a restaurant counter, I am never dragging them off to the Court of Judicial Review again!
"Next time a waiter smiles and asks if my tea's lost its flavor and needs a fresh pot, I am never saying 'sure' and sitting there until closing time again!
"Why can't people just say what they mean?!" The more Blaze thought about it, the angrier she got, until she tossed the cheat sheet and notebook right into the corner of the guest room.
...
Gu Zhuhuang returned to the guest room and checked her luggage one last time. She was leaving Baizao tomorrow. A notebook tucked beneath the curtain in the corner caught her eye. She picked it up, recalling how she was when she first arrived in Baizao.
"Why can't people just say what they mean..." Gu Zhuhuang thought about it carefully. "Turns out, sometimes they really can't."
She dug a pen out of her luggage and, right below the last sentence on that small slip of paper, wrote a reply to her past self.
"Blaze, when you first stepped into Yan, this unfamiliar homeland, it was inevitable to feel anxious and afraid. But once you stopped being afraid and truly saw yourself as one of them, you realized that being straightforward isn't a problem at all. Honesty and courage are virtues in Yan just the same.
"Besides, sometimes the words left unsaid are the ones etched deepest in memory."

uniequip_002_orchd2.desc.text:
Earthspirit arrived at the corner of the training grounds, where she had set up several targets reserved for her personal use—well, she had never actually forbidden anyone else from using them, but everyone assumed they were hers alone; after all, their shapes were far too distinct.
Earthspirit had just finished an excruciating debrief with Op Reserve Team A6. Catapult had gone off on her own again, Spot had submitted a report covered in storyboard drafts for his new manga, and Midnight had tried to smooth things over with a few bar coupons. She felt that familiar tide of irritation rushing over her.
Taking a deep breath, Earthspirit drew her bow.
To her, what she hunted was not beasts, but chaos.
Evidently, returning from the land of mirages hadn't changed her daily life in the slightest, nor could a momentary shift in perspective quench the fury ignited by reality.
Thwack. An arrow struck Spot's chest with pinpoint accuracy. She recalled that sloppy report and that guy's lazy face.
Thwack. An arrow pierced Midnight's collar. She recalled the pungent cologne and his smooth, empty excuses.
Thwack, thwack, thwack. She recalled Catapult's near-suicidal thrill in battle. Her breathing quickened as arrow after arrow flew out, until that target was bristling with shafts.
Then, her eyes landed on the final target. Popukar. Earthspirit drew her bow and took aim.
Popukar was always the child who gave her the biggest headache. Because Popukar stubbornly believed that Team A6 would stay together forever, a conviction that hadn't changed one bit as she grew older.
Sometimes, Popukar's unwavering certainty gave her a fleeting panic that she might be saddled with A6's headaches for the rest of her life.
Still, she stared at Popukar for a long time before taking a deep breath and calming down.
She had never done something like this in the past—she would just lose her temper directly. But she knew losing her temper changed nothing; these people wouldn't reform, and in the end, she had to bottle it all up herself.
Yet after returning from the land of mirages, she decided to try a new approach. To her surprise, none of the A6 members took offense; they even began teasing each other over whether Earthspirit had shot at their target that day. And for her, each shooting session brought a few fresh ideas.
She decided not to scold Spot, but to leave his report unreviewed for now, waiting until he couldn't stand it and came asking on his own.
She decided to pretend to believe Midnight's nonsense, just to see how he'd react if she actually followed his advice.
As for Catapult, well, she had to admit she didn't actually dislike who Catapult was now. If there was anything she could truly do, perhaps it was to hone her skills so she could stop Catapult from taking reckless risks in the future, or... help her? Earthspirit sighed, reluctant to admit she was having such thoughts.
And Popukar—alas, what could Popukar ever do wrong! She was already thinking about what design to use for Popukar's new outfit.
With those thoughts in mind, she happily lowered her bow.
Yes, with her frustration vented, she felt much lighter.
She began to realize that perhaps some things were never as complicated as she had once thought.

uniequip_002_catap2.desc.text:
A dim, damp underground hall. Free from the glitz of the Kazimierz arenas, there was only the stench of blood and the roar of beasts.
A lavishly dressed man stood outside an iron cage, gazing with satisfaction at the giant beast that had just been injected with drugs and was violently slamming into the bars.
"Yes, yes... that's the fury I want! For tomorrow's match, I've bet three million on you. Tear that guy to shreds! Hahahaha!"
Clank. The heavy metal door was pushed open.
The man turned around in panic. "Who's there?!"
A Kuranta woman strode in, bearing a shield on her back and holding a blade in hand, looking every bit like a Knight.
"Which knightclub are you from? I've never seen you before!" the man blustered, trying to mask his fear. "Get out! This is no place for you!"
The Kuranta woman finally came to a halt.
"I heard there was a formidable beast here. I'm here to challenge it."
"Huh? Challenge?" The man sounded as if he had heard the greatest joke in the world, glancing at her gear. "Who do you think you are? The Blood Knight? Or the Radiant Knight? Scram! Or my guards will..."
Several guards lunged from the shadows. Right at that moment, a barrage of arrows shot out from their blind spot, cleanly interrupting the guards' movements. Next, a frivolous-looking Sarkaz man and a shield-bearing Rebbah sprang from the shadows, easily subduing the guards.
Meanwhile, a childish girl's voice came through the Kuranta woman's comms: "Sister Catapult, I've got the door covered! No one's getting in!"
Before the man could even scream, the shield slammed into his chest, pinning him firmly against the wall, knocking him unconscious instantly.
She turned back to face the roaring beast that still lunged at her. Long accustomed to such scenes, she even had the mood to tease the figures stepping out of the dark: "Oh my, Sister Earthspirit, what brings you all here?"
The bow-wielding Liberi woman stepped into the light, rolling her eyes. "You mean to tell me you 'dropped' your plan on the desk so conspicuously, and expected me not to follow along once I saw it? Don't act innocent after getting what you wanted."
"Heh heh." The Kuranta woman rubbed her nose happily. Of course she had done it on purpose; this was her way of roping everyone in A6 into her "hunting venture."
"Honestly, couldn't you pick an easier target?" the Liberi woman grumbled, hunching her shoulders against the chill she despised.
"Can't be helped," the Kuranta woman shrugged. "Who told the fiercest beasts on this land to be the ones without fangs and claws?"
With that, she unlocked the iron cage, while the other three naturally took their places behind her.
"Let's make this quick. It's almost time for Popukar's bedtime."

uniequip_003_shu.desc.text:
Shu walked into that "heart" which had long fallen silent.
Creating this massive machine had cost her and her sisters considerable effort, but ultimately it did not serve as that chess player's grim fallback contingency. Today, it seemed to have become a true heart, tethered at one end to this land tilled for a thousand years, and at the other to a faint consciousness deep within a tomb thousands of miles away—Shu could feel this connection.
Shu wanted to help this heart continue growing, beating. It was not just the people toiling here who needed it—she had a strong premonition, or perhaps wishful thinking, that her "brother" would need it too one day.
Carefully, she channeled her power into the "heart," and then, she fell into a dream filled with the fragrance of blooming rice.
Insects chirped softly. She heard the sounds of all living things—the rustle of tender rice leaves unfurling, the dull thud of roots taking hold in soil, even the sound of storm clouds gathering, whispering right in her ear.
Rain poured down soon after. A hazy figure holding a hoe walked over, took her hand, and led her to dig an irrigation ditch, just like when he first taught her. The water pooled in the fields drained away, but the downpour still scattered the seeds in disarray. Fortunately, the remaining seeds fought to sprout tender yet resilient roots, bursting into new life.
Yet soon, a gale swept across, pounding the fields with hailstones nearly the size of fists. The frail sprouts were torn up by their roots and hurled back into the mud. Amidst the blinding wind, someone handed her a bolt of fabric. She unrolled the cloth to shelter the tottering sprouts and reinforced the trellises with branches, toiling tirelessly. Finally, the wind ceased. She looked up, and the rice plants were already in bloom, fragrant and white. Those tiny blossoms filled the heart with profound joy, yet the buzzing of insect wings ominous arose.
A swarm of locusts blotted out the sky. Shu caught sight of a lone back walking ahead through the near-pitch darkness. A cluster of flame ignited beside him, driving away the relentless swarm. The fire burned brighter and fiercer, until the blackness before her turned crimson.
Looking upon the scattered sprouts, Shu kept the hoe on her shoulder and continued her meticulous care—weeding, watering, fertilizing. Day after day, year after year, through frost and rain, drought and hail, time flowed past her feet like river water. Her hair grew longer and longer, melding into the azure of the river; her skirts were dyed green by grass and brown by soil. She repeated this toil until a muffled voice echoed from beneath the earth.
"You are weary."
"It is rare for you to appear in another's dream. Have you nothing to say, choosing instead to manifest as disasters just to frighten me?"
"I merely wish to tell you: as things stand, these efforts are in vain."
"When you stood alone, wagering against that faint thread of fate, did I ever say your efforts were in vain?"
The deep voice beneath the soil seemed about to speak again, but Shu simply turned and brushed her hand across the green sprouts. As rice blossoms drifted down, two curious wine cups appeared beside her. The sky shifted in color like ink wash; beside her, a meal in a metal lunchbox atop a stone still steamed, and the herbs in her basket bore fresh morning dew. A gentle breeze brushed by like silk, the flora singing like music, the rice rustling as if in harmony. Suddenly, the wind surged as fierce as fists, twisting and turning, before everything mingled with the fine drizzle from the sky and fell into the cups.
"This is wine freshly brewed by Sister Ling this year, made from our dreams—our shared dream."
No one answered, but the other cup of wine slowly drained away, as though someone had drunk it clean. He could taste the fragrance of those dreams; he knew what this cup meant. The taste of hope is always the sweetest.
"I didn't give you those seeds just so you would end up with a result where 'a life is traded for a life.' I am still waiting for that harvest season, for the whole family to enjoy together, with not a single one missing...
"That ought to be a fine season."

uniequip_002_toledo.desc.text:
Kill the ocean.
Every Iberian who yearns to join the Inquisition carries that resolution to some degree, and so do I. But I can only murmur it in my heart, for I hold no rapier—only a spade for planting sugarcane. In every coastal village and town across Iberia, there must be people who share my thoughts. Some joined the Punitive Force; others died. This town is remote; an Inquisitor only comes once every two years on patrol to recruit newcomers. It was that time of year again, but evidently they were late, or perhaps they wouldn't come at all. I've seen the horrors of the Seaborn, and I knew what joining the Punitive Force meant. Yet I needed a real weapon—like an Inquisitor's rapier. I prayed that strength would free me from my terror of the sea, and breathe life back into this forgotten town.
A stranger arrived in town. Not an Inquisitor, but a petite Liberi looking for lodging. She dressed dashingly and bore a lengthy name, seemingly of noble descent. Every day she gave speeches in the square, drawing large crowds whose laughter and wonder echoed all the way to the shore. I cared nothing for her origins; my eyes were fixed on the blade at her hip—a proper weapon, capable of combating the Seaborn and the tides, capable of truly letting someone accomplish something. Sadly, it wasn't mine to wield.
The crowd behind that noble grew larger, gesturing and planning all across town. Getting the mayor's approval took her some effort. I couldn't understand why she didn't simply brandish her blade—was it merely an ornament? The chance to find out came soon enough. The noble stepped into my field, tasting the irrigation water and inspecting the withered sugarcane. If she wished to purchase the land, I would gladly part with it; so long as I could join the Inquisition afterwards, I would never return to this desolate town. Hearing my words, she drew her blade—looking every bit the conquistador now—thrust the fine weapon into the earth, pulled it back out, rubbed the soil on the tip between her fingers, and proposed a trade.
"You want to collateralize your blade for my shovel?"
"That's right, just for a moment."
The noble plunged the shovel into the earth and twisted it—as expected, she was unsuited for farm work, looking utterly clumsy. Yet, the sand slowly darkened, and water began seeping up from beneath, pooling in the pit like a miniature sea.
"There's freshwater underground not far from your field. Connect it to Rhodes Island's irrigation system, and it will keep your bellies full for the coming year. A descendant of the Iberian Royal Navy, the great Lady De Toledo, gives you her word."
"A navy descendant... using a shovel? Farming sugarcane?"
"You care about that? I'm fulfilling my 'noblesse oblige'! Besides, I tried digging with my blade, and it was terribly inefficient. As for you, standing here watching the sea with a shovel every day, did it never cross your mind to dig downward?"
I looked at the field at my feet and the noble blade planted in the dirt, forgetting for a moment the Inquisition and the roaring sea. The noble calling herself De Toledo said she would stay in town, inviting me to join the irrigation team. Perhaps once the sugarcane ripens, I can ask to borrow that blade to peel some stalks.

uniequip_003_vulpis.desc.text:
A pure white handkerchief wiped away the warm droplets of blood from the blade, only to be cast aside onto the corner of the table without a second glance.
Ingrid bandaged her wounds, spread the letters piled at the door across the desk, and slit them open one by one for inspection.
A few damp letters bore discreet wax seals—instructions from the family. She knew they would contain nothing but the same urging for her return to Siracusa, so she didn't even bother reading them.
A few bills: rent, water, heating. Ingrid frowned; she had thought the family's influence would handle such matters during her two months away assassinating targets.
Oh, she realized, this was a warning—such a childish, petty warning. She had no intention of replying to those summons, planning instead to remain in Higashi for a while longer.
The family never spoke with a single voice: some pleaded for her return, while others ceaselessly added fresh names to her hit list.
Regardless, she didn't care. If there was a mission, she would carry it out. It was just killing people, after all.
She picked up the next envelope. Just as she was about to tear it down the middle, her fingertips recognized the unique texture of the paper and the delicate watermark of flowers and vines.
She rummaged through her room until she found a letter opener.
"The snow on the mountain peak has begun to melt. Brewing tea with snowmelt, sitting across to gaze at the view, the scenery is lovely."
She set the letter down, then picked it up again, reading it once in Higashinese and once in Siracusan. Checking the postmark on the envelope, she suddenly walked to the window, striving to make out the distant peak.
The far-off mountain was vibrant with lush greenery.
"Halt!" At the foot of the mountain, a shrine guard barred Ingrid's path.
She did not halt; she simply swung her sword.
One stroke, then another.
Fewer and fewer dared to step forward, and she climbed higher and higher up the mountain.
The freshly bandaged wounds tore open once more, blood seeping through the white gauze and blooming crimson across her coat like vivid camellias.
At last, she reached the mountain peak.
The snow had melted long ago, yet that person was still brewing a pot of tea. The young priest invited her to sit, but she shook her head.
She meant that she was drenched in blood, and the stench of it would ruin the tea.
The priest shook his head as well, meaning the tea mattered little. Ingrid understood, and sat down before a stone tea table in the courtyard.
They sat in silence, their gazes sweeping over the peak where the snow had vanished, over the petals fluttering in the courtyard, and over the drops of blood along the mountain trail—
Nearly all of it was her own blood, welling from wounds sustained while killing for the family, wounds that had never truly healed.
Finally, she spoke: "I've grown tired of blood. I want to see the snow from your letter."
The young priest nodded. Dipping his finger into the tea, he seemed about to write something on the table, but withdrew his hand.
A few days later, Ingrid received another letter. She opened it with the letter opener; inside was likewise a single line.
"Western attire, sword dance; the fair lady intoxicated amidst mountain flowers."
She folded the letter and laid it across the blade.

uniequip_003_qiubai.desc.text:
The vessel slipped past the Ghost Gate Shoals four times before finally beaching. Watching the shadows lengthen over the mountains, the crew dove into the water to haul cargo without catching their breath. The winter river was bone-chilling, yet not a single face betrayed hardship—with this haul, they wouldn't have to worry through the new year.
"The master is at the stern. Watch your footing, miss, don't trip over the crates."
The one shouting was a white-bearded elder, still doing bloodstained business on this river well into his seventies.
"Second Uncle, have you seen Master Xu?"
The girl squeezed through the noisy throng, frantically scanning the dim riverbank.
"Looking for Little Xu, miss? Hmm, saw him on board during the day, but right now, I'm afraid—"
"Save your breath, miss! That fellow fell into the water with the escorts!"
Beside them, several lightly dressed water bandits were dragging a beast of burden ashore by its horns. The leader tossed out those words before turning back to calculate the creature's weight with his brothers.
The girl froze in place, locking eyes with the drenched beast of burden.

"Come on, cheers!"
Darkness swallowed the river, yet the water fortress blazed with light. Laughter rolled across the floor as jug after jug was emptied. Though bonfires blazed, she felt only cold.
She had sharpened that sword carefully of late; it now rested inside a scrap of white cloth left over from her mother's sewing.
Yet the one who taught her the sword would never return! He had promised to teach her the next stance come the new year—
"Why so downcast, miss?"
Second Uncle was thoroughly drunk, his face flushed crimson.
"*Hic*. Don't worry, don't worry. Look at the fires, look at the goods! Even if the snow buries our doors, we're bound for a prosperous new year!"
He patted the girl's shoulder, trying to pull her into the revelry. She gazed into the fire reflected in their eyes—foggy, yet brighter than any flame lit since the start of winter. Laughter, drums, and drinking games swallowed the whole fortress, while not a soul mentioned the young man swallowed by the river. But, she thought, but...
Everyone lived so passionately, so why didn't they save him? Why did none of them ever utter the word "death"?
She slipped out of the main hall and walked all the way beneath the bamboo pavilion to the east. Suddenly, she spotted a patch of white. Looking closer, it was the beast hauled ashore earlier. Fed with hay and its coat dried, it now lay peacefully in the shed, mooing contentedly toward her. The call was soft and lingering, yet a strange bitterness welled in her heart. Counting the days, the winter solstice had passed and the new year was near; this beast had only a few days left to live.
...It probably didn't know, did it?
Yet this life, this death, how one lives, why one dies, and what follows after... forget beasts, among the people living by this river, who truly understood any of it?

The next morning, snow had begun to fall. In the blink of an eye, the towering dark peaks on both banks were cloaked in solemn frost. The main hall was desolate and cold, the revelers long gone, with cups, plates, and bowls scattered askew across the floor. The girl looked down and saw a murky ice flower frozen inside the dregs of wine, looking just like the white plum blossom she had struck into the mud with a sword stroke after the rain that day. She picked up the bowl, walked to the riverbank, and cast the remaining wine along with the white cloth wrapping the sword into the water.
The wine and the white cloth drifted downstream...
White was not merely snow, nor was it merely blossoms.

uniequip_003_narant.desc.text:
"She's no good person!"
Two runaway girls were lost in the wilderness, the sky dim and direction impossible to discern.
"That red-haired lunatic snatched us from those sand bandits just to sell us to other ones!"
Ayaji and Ayani were not biological sisters, but slaves captured from different places by the sand bandits; even their names were made up by themselves.
"But she cut our shackles and gave us food."
"An act! She keeps babbling about tribal codes just to get us to let our guard down."
"Ayaji, I can't run anymore! I want to go back. Following her means at least we won't starve."
"Even if you're a bandit, you ought to follow a boss with a future! Look at her—she doesn't even have a single follower. What kind of future does that hold?"
"But she said she used to have plenty of followers, only they didn't want to follow her anymore, so she decided never to be a boss again."
"Then why don't you think about why they didn't want to follow her?!"
Engrossed in their bickering, they failed to notice a pack of roaming riftbeasts closing in silently.
"O-Oh no! Ayaji, I don't want to die here!"
The riftbeast matriarch circled them, seemingly waiting for something. The other riftbeasts began roaring into the distance. Soon, a red silhouette appeared.
"Didn't I tell you there were riftbeasts around, and not to run off while I went to buy supplies?"
"I thought you were just scaring us so we wouldn't escape!"
"Escape? If you want to leave, leave. When did I ever stop you?"
Panting, Narentuya handed each of them a whip and a dagger, then stepped forward. The game of predator and prey shifted into a standoff between two packs.
"You want to keep your pack alive, and so do I. They are my people. We will fight back, and I will kill the beasts in your pack—two, three, I can definitely take down. If you want mutual ruin, let's have at it."
The riftbeast matriarch fell silent.
"Doesn't seem worth it to you, huh?" Narentuya spat. "Then beat it!"
The provoked beasts roared in unison, and Narentuya screamed back at the top of her lungs, answering with her own defiance.
Only when all the beasts retracted their fangs did Narentuya stop. She tossed out a pouch she had just purchased, containing salt essential for the beasts.
The matriarch took the salt pouch in her jaws and led her pack back into the depths of the wasteland.
"Let's go home," Narentuya said, her voice hoarse. "Now that I've taken you in as my crew, you listen to me from now on. No more running off."
"W-When did you take us in? And didn't you say you'd never be a boss again?"
"Can't help it. I didn't want to be a boss either, but I couldn't just watch you die, could I? If you don't like it, I can call the beasts back."
Ayaji kept her mouth shut. Ayani leaned in and whispered, "A boss who can scare off a pack of riftbeasts is definitely going places."
Ayaji sighed. "We both owe her our lives now. How are we supposed to repay that? We can't be her crew forever, can we?"
"Ayaji, this is already the second time she's saved us. A lifetime might not even be enough."
Without looking back, Narentuya replied, "I don't need your payback, and I don't have the patience to be someone's boss for a lifetime! When we part ways someday and you've found a peaceful life, just remembering me is enough. Sending a small gift during holidays would be nice, too."
"Don't worry, Boss! We'll send you the best gifts!"
"...No need to plan for our parting just yet."

uniequip_003_ulpia.desc.text:
It was pitch black here; around the trench, every rock looked identical. He had been away from the cities for too long; behind him, the distant, glorious Aegir had shrunk to a tiny speck of light. Before him, the Seaborn emitted a faint luminescence, swelling its fluid sacs and extending soft tentacles to grasp his arm, which he easily dodged. It seemed unsure of where to go, hovering in place as its dim glow pulsed at a steady rhythm. Spreading its folded mantle, it sensed the direction of the We Many within the currents. Then the creature turned to him, uttering garbled sounds resembling broken Aegir, calling him to feel the direction of the We Many together. It gurgled, slowly addressing him as... "kin."
"I do not understand your way of communicating," he replied. "I am not one of you."
The Seaborn drifted its limbs; the guidance from the We Many was indistinct, and its light dimmed somewhat. He sighed softly and subconsciously touched his inner pocket, pulling out a circular piece of metal—a water compass of his own design, entirely mechanical to avoid any interference from the Seaborn. Built specifically for the Abyssal Hunters, its purpose was plain to the point of austerity: to faithfully point the way home, no matter what.
Yet the sensitive needle, which ought to have swayed briskly to ascertain bearings, remained stuck, pointing silently and obstinately in a single direction.

"How did it break? Smashed against a rock outcropping?" Brandus stared at the water compass in his hand. "You should have used a sturdier resin back then." His old friend spread his hands helplessly. "Custom-made for the Abyssal Hunters—once these little things break, there's one fewer in the world."
He wiped away Seaborn fluids splattered across his clothes. "No need to fix it." Reaching out, he tucked the water compass back into his inner pocket, revealing unhealed old wounds on his forearm. Brandus stared at his scars, silent for a moment, then spoke: "...'Researchers always resemble their creations.' Has anyone ever told you that?"
He impassively wiped away the blood from where the wound had reopened. "You really should have been a poet."
Brandus raised an eyebrow, taking the quip in stride before returning to organizing the hunters' biometric data. After a long pause, the usually taciturn man broke the silence.
"...At least I can still move for now," he said.

Ahead, the Seaborn seemed to figure out where to go. Its tentacles twined around his arm, tugging him downward. He pulled his arm free, remaining motionless, and opened that water compass one last time. It was long broken, cracked, its alloy dulled without its original luster, his name engraved upon it barely legible; yet the needle still stubbornly pointed toward Aegir. It had accompanied him on countless missions, pointing toward Aegir time and again, though his sense of direction was keen enough to find the way home no matter how far he strayed.
If our fates truly are this alike... Ulpianus closed the lid of the water compass and returned it to his inner pocket. He drew his coat tight, followed the Seaborn ahead, and descended deeper into the ocean trench.

uniequip_002_makoto.desc.text:
One afternoon, under the blazing sun, Giada pointed toward the warehouse ahead. Giulio and Makoto Yuki pulled up the roll-up door together with all their strength.
Inside, it was cool. Giada walked up to a row of storage shelves and said, "These were hers." Giada told Giulio to inspect everything on the nearby table, while Yuki stood beside Giulio, helping him pack the items he decided to keep into cardboard boxes.
"This is..." Giulio opened a storage box and marvelled, "What an old song."
He asked Giada, "Are these all tapes collected by Auntie? Did you listen to them when going through her effects?" Giada shook her head. "Not all of them... and not all of them were collections."
Giada sorted out a few plain-looking tapes and said, "These should be recordings she made herself. I mentioned to Yuki that I heard a song among her effects, and this is where it was." Yuki seemed a little perplexed, while Giulio asked curiously, "Which one? I want to hear it too."
After a brief hesitation, Giada picked out a tape, inserted it into the radio nearby, plugged it in, and pressed play.
The home-recorded cassette hissed with static. Unaccompanied, a slightly hoarse woman's voice sang a tender, affectionate melody, bringing Giulio close to tears. The afternoon sunlight poured into the warehouse, the dazzling white light rippling across the floor like water.
"...Candy, guns, and faith, I drink Laterano to the dregs." He quietly sang along to the final lines.
The music faded, and surprisingly, Yuki was the first to speak: "I remember now, what Miss Giada said back then... So, your insistence regarding the funeral, was it really about this song?"
Giada replied, "...Yeah. This tape was probably recorded not long ago... But basing the deceased's wishes on merely how I felt hearing a song was perhaps too presumptuous of me."
Yuki shook his head. "Music truly can tell us a lot of things."
"...Speaking of which, Yuki seems to listen to music quite often, doesn't he?" Giulio lowered his head to wipe his eyes, his usual smile returning.
"Well..." Yuki was caught off guard by the sudden shift of topic to himself, while Giada let out a quiet sigh of relief. Giulio asked again, "What kind of songs do you usually listen to, Yuki?"
"...I can let everyone hear them, if you'd like." Yuki turned on his portable player and showed it to them.
"Actually, does listening to the same song feel a bit like empathy?" Giulio rubbed his chin and mused aloud.
"Except for you, nobody here knows what empathy feels like..." Giada couldn't help saying.
"...I think I might understand," Yuki answered earnestly.
Suddenly, Giada remembered something. On that day, that very dusk, what she had felt. At the very end, she had indeed heard music—the sound of a cello, like starlight, like the evening glow.
"...Then perhaps, I've felt it too," Giada said.
"Right? Music is a feeling you can hear," Giulio smiled gently.
"There has always been a way to understand how others feel," Yuki looked at Giulio and said with conviction. "There are many things that can connect us all together."
"As long as moments like that have existed, they will never truly fade away," he said.

uniequip_002_aigis.desc.text:
Somewhere on the grounds of Saint Marceau Comprehensive School, a school custodian sat on the steps, petting a listless Cloudbeast.
"Did that student not come today?" the custodian asked. The Cloudbeast brushed its tail against the empty food bowl by the flower bed, let out a displeased whine, then suddenly twitched its ears and took a few steps forward.
Aigis, dressed in her novice habit, arrived in a hurry, politely asking, "Hello, could you please excuse me?"
"It's been waiting for you for a long time," the custodian shifted a few inches and replied with a smile.
"There was a performance for the drama festival today, so I arrived late... But, do you know me?" Aigis asked the elderly woman before her, taking a small pouch of Cloudbeast food from her pouch and pouring it into the bowl. The Cloudbeast immediately trotted over.
"I just often see you feeding this Cloudbeast. You two are on quite good terms," the custodian replied, grooming the Cloudbeast's fur.
"Is that so? I thought it did not like me very much." Aigis still remembered the first time she met the Cloudbeast; it had dodged her touch. Fuuka said that feeding it might bring them closer. Aigis took the advice, but had never tried to pet it again.
"Really? But it's been waiting for you all this time. Did you buy this bowl?" The custodian looked at the Cloudbeast burying its head in the bowl, eating voraciously.
"I bought it. I saw it in a shop and thought it resembled it a little..." It wasn't a difficult question, yet Aigis's voice sounded somewhat hesitant. Perhaps because she had never thought this Cloudbeast actually liked her, leaving her unsure how to respond amidst the surprise.
"Since you didn't come today, it kept circling around this bowl. Maybe it feels that this bowl represents a 'promise.'" The custodian smiled warmly.
"Perhaps it was merely hungry..." Aigis said. The Cloudbeast, having finished eating, uncharacteristically did not leave, but rubbed against Aigis's shins and nudged her with its head.
"Go ahead and pet it," the custodian suggested. After a moment's hesitation, Aigis reached out a finger and stroked the top of the Cloudbeast's head.
"However, I will be leaving before long. If it thinks a 'promise' has been made..." Aigis's voice trailed off.
"I see..." the custodian said. "Then after you leave, I'll help you out. I can use your bowl, right?"
"...You would help me?" Aigis was somewhat surprised. She actually remembered this elderly woman, but had never spoken with her. Just as she had never spoken with many of the people she had seen.
"Hehe, if you feel bad about it, how about watering this flower bed for me before you leave? If you make a promise with me, I will promise to keep feeding it. By Laterano rules, an exchange of promises—that should settle it, right?" Sensing Aigis's stiffness, the custodian smiled and told her.
An exchange of promises...
The Cloudbeast meowed softly. Snapping back to reality, Aigis nodded solemnly and said, "...Of course. No, thank you very much."
So a promise is something that connects people to people, and people to things, that previously had no connection. Aigis thought.
The custodian looked at the child, whose face was full of seriousness and thought, and smiled faintly. The Cloudbeast rubbed against Aigis again; she reached out with a finger, then switched to her open palm, gently stroking the Cloudbeast's back. The sunlight warmed the creature's coat. When would spring come to an end? she wondered.

uniequip_002_yukari.desc.text:
On the day off following the drama festival, the class representative knocked on the dormitory door holding a massive tote bag.
Moments later, in Yukari's room, Yukari in her Garrison uniform and Fuuka in her Gunsmith attire stood before Amiya's camera lens.
"It looks great! I wonder how the Doctor managed to convince Closure to let us keep these costumes." Amiya adjusted the framing on her camera, looking quite pleased.
Yukari and Fuuka glanced at each other and couldn't help laughing together. Fuuka adjusted Yukari's hat and said, "Yukari was thinking of what happened before too, wasn't she?" Amiya, about to snap a photo of them laughing, looked over curiously upon hearing this.
Yukari waved her hand. "It's nothing, really, just something from back in our world. Because the school festival was cancelled, I dragged Fuuka into my room to try on the maid outfits we were originally going to wear for it."
"Though the maid outfit was very cute back then... this Garrison uniform really suits Yukari, given her talent with archery," Fuuka said.
Amiya looked at the two in the viewfinder and suddenly remarked, "Actually... just hypothetically, if you stayed in Laterano, I think Yukari would be quite well-suited for joining the Garrison."
"Huh... Can foreigners join too?" Yukari tilted her head inquisitively.
"Returning Sankta can, and the Doctor seems to know people like that; if others can obtain Lateran citizenship, it might be possible too? ...Still, it's just a hypothesis, I just thought it really suited you." Amiya captured the moment Yukari tilted her head and replied.
Yukari pondered: "Come to think of it, the Garrison member I played was originally just a pilgrim, too... In the final scene, as she stands on the city walls looking out over all of Laterano, the narrator calls her arrival here a 'reward of fate'—which probably referred to her becoming a Garrison member as well."
"For that character to become a Garrison member, it was fate at work..." Fuuka murmured, her expression growing somewhat melancholic.
"Ah, I don't see it that way... What I actually meant was, that character must have put in enough hard work to earn that final reward," Yukari continued. "If fate could arbitrarily decide our futures, that would be terrible, wouldn't it? What would our efforts even mean then? If someone told me 'the school festival being cancelled by a typhoon was fate's arrangement,' I wouldn't just accept that."
Amiya listened quietly to their words. If this encounter with them was a reward of fate, it was fleeting and illusory. When the friends before her returned to their original world, would they even remember this place... The Doctor had mentioned that they might forget everything upon returning, as the severance of causality across worlds would smooth out the vibrations of informational waves. If atonement was destined to be forgotten, what did it really atone for?
Yukari looked out the window. It was a clear, sunny day, with Beastfowl gliding gracefully across the building rooftops.
"Just like the pilgrim herself said: face your heart honestly and do the right thing, and along the path forward you will meet the person you've been waiting for... That is true fate, and only that can be called a reward."
She broke into a bright smile, and Fuuka was infected by her warmth. Watching their smiling faces, Amiya nodded gently yet firmly.

uniequip_002_aphris.desc.text:
The Originium circuit improvement plan for drones submitted by Lorenz a few weeks ago had already become reality, achieving undeniably stellar results across multiple performance metrics.
This was not a project a thirteen-year-old child should have been involved in. Yet in a place like Tacoma, children whose parents were researchers could hardly find anything more entertaining than studying, while many researchers themselves hoped to take on positions where they didn't have to deal with disease and death every single day. Although the counseling team strove to propose all kinds of leisure activities to make life here more relaxed and comfortable, in a small town "focused on medical services," an oppressive atmosphere still inevitably lingered—one where having too much fun felt almost like doing something wrong.
And so, as long as a student was willing to learn, teachers dared to teach. This instructional approach, vastly different from standard educational models, was nothing new in Tacoma, nor was Lorenz the only youthful face to appear in institutions of higher education. Furthermore, she was the child of "that Robert."
"Still, Professor, I don't quite understand," Lorenz said, watching the drone's flight path thoughtfully. "You said I shouldn't use my Originium Arts to directly manipulate the Originium chip in real time to achieve optimization, so I spent over a year learning how to achieve a similar effect with Originium circuits."
"Yes, because your unique Originium Arts cannot be mass-produced like Originium circuits, meaning it cannot become a mature technology suitable for widespread application."
"But I found that you were wrong—we were both wrong. This isn't a good enough research topic." Lorenz wore a genuine smile, the kind a child would have for their own masterpiece, though it made the professor feel somewhat uneasy. "As a control, I also tried using Originium Arts to write partial computational logic into several pieces of Originium respectively. After integrating them into the circuit and debugging with an inverter, I believe it is practically equivalent to imitating Originium Arts."
"Perhaps so... but you shouldn't have done that. There is still so much about Originium Arts we haven't uncovered; doing this is truly dangerous."
"Yes, Originium Arts is like a black box. We seem able to channel energy to achieve what we want without understanding the principles behind it. So after this past year of learning, I am even more convinced that Originium can, to a certain degree, receive and realize our will, whether or not we ourselves possess sufficient knowledge regarding the process of its realization."
"Treating Originium as a wish-granting machine of unknown principles is not the rigorous attitude one should take toward science."
"Therefore, my hypothesis is that the medium Originium relies on when interacting with matter or energy is the same as the one it relies on when receiving instructions: neither wave nor particle, its nature is like a ghost, or rather, 'information.' This explains why we observe no discernible changes in mass or energy when Originium is utilized. I imagine I'm not the first person to propose this hypothesis, but don't you think this is the truly valuable research topic of our era?"
"...You had already formed this hypothesis long before you attended my class, didn't you?"
"Yes. That was the first time I fiddled with an Originium camera, when I saw my late father in the viewfinder."
"I'm sorry."
"No, Professor, that is not the rigorous attitude one should take toward science." The girl's expression remained completely unchanged. "I am glad my hypothesis received preliminary validation, and I am willing to travel much further down this road."

uniequip_002_hbound.desc.text:
Nacho woke up well before dawn. He had to sweep away the dust blown in from the sea that coated the windows, tidy up the tools his grandmother had scattered across the floor yesterday, mend holes of all sizes in the scale nets, and bring the kettle of rainwater outside to the stove. Only after all of this was done would he sit by the window, staring silently at his fish tank.
Staring at the city inside the tank.
A model of an Aegirian city, one he had placed inside just a few days ago. Next to the tank sat over a dozen older models he had taken out previously. Making these models had long become a habit for Nacho.
Why?
Perhaps because his grandmother always said they did not belong here. He didn't know where he belonged, but he tried his hardest to imagine it.
He would point to his newly finished models and describe the underwater life he envisioned to his grandmother. Spherical living pods that could be recombined at will, or floating districts entirely interconnected by pipelines...
Of course, at that time he didn't know that his grandmother had long forgotten what the cities of Aegir looked like. Wearily chiming in with his descriptions, she simply couldn't bring herself to interrupt him.
The models piled higher and higher on the windowsill. Which one did the real cities of Aegir actually resemble? He didn't know, but he had tried so hard to imagine—to imagine what a place of shelter, a home of one's own, ought to look like.
Clemence looked at the rows of city models on the windowsill, making no attempt to conceal her astonishment.
"Such design talent... with a bit of training, you truly could work in urban design."
"Supervisor Clemence, me?"
"Of course, Nacho. If you do not wish to go to Aegir, you can complete all the design work right here, and then one day in the future, watch the city you designed with your own hands rise above the distant sea."
"I'm honored, thank you, but... I can't really tell if I'm still seriously designing these buildings anymore..."
Nacho stared at the model in the tank. Tiny fish swarmed in small groups, weaving through its gaps and hollows.
"These hollow architectural structures... unlike before, I can no longer explain how I imagined them, or why I designed them that way. I suppose... it's just so the fish in the tank can swim through them. The tank was their home to begin with, so if my models go in and do nothing for them, that would just be awful."
"So, what is your decision?"
"I think I'll pass. These models... let's just pretend they aren't some grand cities of Aegir, but merely shelter for these little fish. Look... there are even fish eggs sticking to it."

uniequip_002_thumpy.desc.text:
"Aahh... I can't eat all this! I'm only leaving for five or six days, you don't need such a grand farewell party..." That was her own flustered voice.
"What did you say, little Thumpy—isn't roasted meat with carrots enough?!" That was Dad's voice, almost drowned out by the noise in the kitchen.
"Eh..." Tani remembered why she fell silent here. Dad's roasted meat with carrots was her absolute favorite dish, but she immediately realized she wouldn't be able to eat the next day's braised meat bones with wild herbs. Travelling far was always exciting, but "leaving home" still brought a twinge of melancholy.
"All the dishes are served! The send-off banquet begins—" That was Mom's cheerful voice, followed by the thudding footsteps of the whole big family drawing close. Tani was instantly engulfed by chirping, enthusiastic well-wishes; her ears were buzzing so loudly back then that she couldn't make out what they were saying, and she still couldn't hear it clearly now. But she could guess—it was nothing more than stay safe on the road, bring back local specialties, remember to reply to messages, and the like.
She must have noticed Dad looking a bit uneasy back then.
"Little Thumpy, uh..." Dad stammered, so unlike his usual self. "Tell us the gift you really want. Me, your mom, your uncles, aunts, cousins... we're all ready to listen to your voice seriously."
...
So the house had been quiet for that long. Then she heard a snicker—it was herself bursting into laughter.
"Dad, your apology is so awkward, and you even dragged so many people along just to build up your courage."
"Ahem..."
"But I don't want a new gift. Even if I'm not a switchboard operator anymore, I still want to cherish everyone's heart in giving me birthday gifts."
"But..."
"Mom, didn't you promise to listen to my voice this time? Actually, I just need everyone to do me a favor~ Well, even though I'm leaving soon, if the whole family works together, we can definitely finish it before I set off!"
In a desolate wind-eroded hollow, Tani was comfortably lounging on her massaging rocking chair. She took a bite of a carrot cracker, topped with a layer of caramel boiled down from throat lozenges. Well, throat lozenges certainly had an odd flavor, and the caramel was a little too burnt, but it matched her clumsy yet lovable cousins perfectly. Beneath her was a super cool contraption fitted with an Originium internal combustion engine and off-road tires—the Massaging Rocking Chair Vehicle. She had driven this big machine all the way here; once she arrived at her destination and detached the outer shell, it turned into a picnic chair with massage functions. Although the shell glued together wasn't very sturdy, and the seat rocked so wildly while driving that she nearly threw up on the console, the process of making it together with everyone was truly so much fun.
And... the headphones from Mom and Dad, along with a switchboard junction box specially modified to adapt to a music player. She wanted to pick it up to listen to some music, only to discover this noisy recording that had been accidentally preserved.

uniequip_002_tmslot.desc.text:
Dear Mom,
(Previous text omitted)
I'm sorry, Mom, I must have disappointed you. I still didn't dare to sign up. You said my grades were passable... but my luck has always been terrible. The takeoff success rate of "Little Flyer" is still very low; even if it barely manages to fly, what if it loses control at the competition venue, knocks off the professor's toupee, or (large section of water-blurred handwriting)—you know I've always been unlucky. But you're right, I'll observe my classmates and professors more to see how they solve problems.
(Subsequent text omitted)
Dearest Mom,
You won't believe this! The day after sending the last letter, I went and registered for the competition~ It started with a small spark of inspiration; I improved the wings of "Little Flyer," barely nudging its takeoff success rate up to—50%... Then, I tried using a classmate's trick: placing *Fluid Dynamics* on my lap, repainting the core components cherry red, and counting to seven before flicking the switch. I felt it—the takeoff success rate was definitely a tiny bit higher than 50%! Luck calibration is part of science too, right? Hehe, so I couldn't resist signing up.
(Subsequent text omitted)
My Good Mom,
I didn't expect you to worry so much that you'd write to Dad asking him to encourage me too. Don't worry, I don't lack confidence, and I'm definitely not superstitious! It's just that, if the chances of success and failure are fifty-fifty, when I step onto the stage, the result will always end up being the failing half. Right now my skills aren't enough, what else do you want me to do... At least performing little rituals before each experiment gives me peace of mind. It feels a bit like when my friends laughed at my soot-covered hands from welding as a child, and you patted my back telling me not to cry—hehe. Of course, I'll continue improving my design, don't you worry.
Wait, it suddenly hit me: I can't do all those unnecessary antics at the competition venue! Why didn't I think of that when I signed up?! Ahhhh! It's over... (water-blurred handwriting)
(Subsequent text omitted)
Mom!
You've probably seen the award certificate I enclosed with the letter by now! It's so great that it arrived safely! You know what? "Little Flyer" took off steadily right under the watchful eyes of the judges and spectators! Painting it cherry red, hiding a control valve in my pocket, and eating carrots without peeling the skin for breakfast really do bring good luck! But... I also have a tiny hope: could it be that every time I refined my skills, I made that other 50% probability infinitesimally small? Could it be, in fact, that what makes up for a lack of luck is my own skill? Could it even be possible that one day, I truly will accomplish great things?
Ugh... I always start daydreaming the moment I taste a bit of sweetness. One should stay humble and cautious! But daydreaming once in a while is okay too, and you'll dream along with me, right, Mom?
...Of course, the little rituals still have to continue. Technological advancement needs luck too, hehe.

uniequip_002_jcinta.desc.text:
"Long-ears and short-ears, welcome to Rim Billiton's 34th Modified Vehicle Race!
"Whether it's modified from an abandoned minecart or driven straight from your family's bottle-tree sap transporter, as long as you can get the vehicle moving, you can enter the track and show off your tuning ingenuity and driving skills! Without further ado, let's take a look at this year's contestants—hm? This little white car looks completely ordinary from the outside. Miss Driver, may I ask what your modification concept was?"
"Hehe, secret for now! I'll tell you after I take first place!"
"Haha, that confident? Then we look forward to your performance! Alright, racers in position—and the race begins!"
(Roar of several engines)
"Whoa, that plainest-looking little white car unexpectedly surged right to the front—tremendous explosive power! Looks like both that young lady's skills and the vehicle's powertrain are formidable! Next up is the obstacle course—impressive shock absorption and stability, whoever tuned this car is not to be underestimated! Several consecutive sharp turns, a real test of driving skill and chassis agility—hm? What are those little flying bugs suddenly swarming out from the car? They look like mechanical devices, seemingly assisting with terrain scanning—a flawless drift through the turn, what a fascinating modification! The little white car has left its competitors far behind, could the victory already be decided?!
"—Wait, an unexpected incident! Swerving to avoid a sandbeast that suddenly darted onto the track, the little white car slammed on the brakes and got jammed between the guardrails! Fortunately, the driver climbed out quickly and appears unhurt, but can she continue? The lead she built up is shrinking fast, is she about to lose the championship?!
"—Whoa! She ran to the stands and borrowed something that looks like a crowbar! Is she planning to pry the car loose and keep driving? Can she really pull that off? That parasol must be something special too! The driver is back in the car, restarting, sprinting—first place! An indisputable first place!"
(Tumultuous cheering)
"Our champion, please give us your victory speech! Hey, hey, hey, why are you snatching my microphone—"
"Phew, phew, everyone! Did you see that?! The solid craftsmanship, the perfect design, the capability to claim first place—all of it comes from the dedicated craftsmanship of engineer Amelia! Of course, even more extraordinary than all of that is her specialty, remote communication technology! And as her investor, I have absolute faith that she will succeed! We've co-founded a telecommunications company, and everyone is welcome to learn more!"
"Wait a minute, you're supposed to give an acceptance speech, not run an advertisement!"
